summary: Proposes a small change to how TCP grows its congestion window: base the increase on the number of previously unacknowledged bytes each acknowledgment covers, rather than adding a fixed amount per acknowledgment. This improves performance and closes a hole receivers could use to push a sender to send faster. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: TCP speeds up each time it hears back. This tweak counts how much each reply actually confirms, so tricks like many tiny replies do not fool it.

questions: tcp congestion window increase per ack
what is tcp appropriate byte counting
what is the limit l in tcp abc
subtitle: Grow TCP's congestion window by the bytes each ACK covers, not by the number of ACKs that arrive.

tldr.problem: TCP traditionally grows its congestion window by a fixed amount per arriving ACK. Delayed ACKs slow that growth, and a misbehaving receiver can send many tiny ACKs to make the sender speed up too fast.
tldr.mechanism: The sender counts the previously unacknowledged bytes each ACK covers and grows the window in proportion. In slow start the per-ACK increase is capped by a limit L, which MUST NOT exceed 2*SMSS.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends ABC with L=1*SMSS for all TCP stacks and encourages experiments with L=2*SMSS. It is an Experimental RFC.

today: RFC 3465 is an Experimental RFC and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its Statement of Intent says the aim was to encourage deployment and a later Proposed Standard.

sections.title: Introduction and Goal
sections.content:
RFC 3465 proposes a small change to how a TCP sender increases its congestion window (cwnd). Instead of basing the increase on the number of acknowledgments (ACKs) that arrive, as RFC 2581 describes, the increase is based on the number of bytes those ACKs acknowledge. The RFC calls this Appropriate Byte Counting (ABC).

The RFC says the change improves performance by reducing the effect of delayed ACKs on window growth, and gives a more measured response to ACKs that cover less than a full segment. The cost is that in some cases it sends larger bursts of segments, which can raise the drop rate.

The document carries a Statement of Intent: the algorithm is understood to be effective and safe but not widely deployed, and the Transport Area intended to resubmit it as a Proposed Standard after more experience.
sections.eli5: Instead of counting how many replies come back, TCP counts how much stuff each reply says arrived. That is a fairer way to decide how fast to go.

sections.title: The Modified Window Increase
sections.content:
TCP uses two phases to grow cwnd. Congestion avoidance grows it linearly. Slow start grows it exponentially, at the start of a transfer or after a retransmission timeout.

In congestion avoidance, the sender stores the bytes ACKed in a bytes_acked variable. When bytes_acked becomes greater than or equal to cwnd, it is reduced by cwnd and cwnd grows by one full-sized segment (SMSS). This opens the window by at most 1 segment per round-trip time, which RFC 2581 allows.

In slow start, a sender SHOULD increase cwnd by the number of previously unacknowledged bytes each ACK covers, provided the increase is not more than a limit L. If the ACK covers 1*SMSS or less, or L is 1*SMSS or less, this is no more aggressive than RFC 2581.
sections.eli5: Every time TCP has heard back about a whole window's worth of data, it adds one more segment to its speed. In the fast-start phase, it adds as much as the reply confirms, up to a cap.

sections.title: Choosing the Limit L
sections.content:
The limit L controls how aggressive slow start is. With L=1*SMSS the behavior is no more aggressive than RFC 2581, and the RFC says ABC SHOULD still be used because it is more conservative in key ways. Implementations MAY use L=2*SMSS and MUST NOT use L greater than 2*SMSS. A very large L could cause line-rate bursts when many ACKs are lost or the receiver sends stretch ACKs.

During slow start after a retransmission timeout, a TCP MUST use L=1*SMSS. An ACK then may cover a lot of previously unacknowledged data without showing that much data left the network. The RFC's example: segment N is dropped, N+1 and N+2 arrive, and the ACK after the retransmission covers N+2, yet only one segment really left the network.

The RFC also notes that ABC never grows cwnd by more than the bytes an ACK covers, so it stays within the limit of no more than doubling cwnd in successive round trips.
sections.eli5: There is a speed limit on how much TCP may add at once. After a scare, such as a timeout, the limit is the smallest, because the replies can be misleading.

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages
sections.content:
ACK counting adds a constant per ACK, even for an interactive session whose ACKs cover only a few bytes. A later large transfer could then go out as a line-rate burst. ABC grows the window in proportion to data actually acknowledged.

Delayed ACKs let a receiver skip ACKs; it SHOULD ACK every second full-sized segment and MUST NOT withhold an ACK for more than 500 ms. ABC with L=2*SMSS roughly negates that slowdown, and also softens the effect of lost ACKs. The RFC cites simulation studies showing higher throughput, especially for short transfers that never leave initial slow start.

The main disadvantages with L=2*SMSS are more burstiness and a small increase in the loss rate. The number of segments sent per ACK rises by at most 1, for example from 2 back-to-back segments to 3. Slow start roughly doubles the window every RTT rather than growing it about 1.5 times. Because of the extra drops, the RFC suggests implementing ABC together with selective acknowledgments (RFC 2018).
sections.eli5: Counting bytes helps TCP speed up faster when replies are skipped, but it can send things in slightly bigger bunches, which may make a few more packets get lost.

sections.title: Fairness and Security
sections.content:
An ACK division attack has a receiver send several ACKs for each data segment, each covering a small part of it. Under ACK counting, this makes the sender grow cwnd too quickly. Under ABC, growth depends on bytes acknowledged, so the attack does not work. The RFC suggests using ABC for this reason even with L=1*SMSS.

On fairness, simulations cited by the RFC show that ABC raises the drop rate of the ABC connection, but competing traffic is not greatly affected. The RFC admits the simulations are not necessarily realistic and encourages more experimentation.
sections.eli5: A cheater used to be able to send tiny replies to trick TCP into speeding up. Counting bytes means tiny replies add only tiny amounts.
